The Trump administration’s unnecessary war didn't just shake the global order — it hit countries where it hurt most, leaving a trail of economic wreckage that will take years to repair.

Chile, which imports nearly all its fuel, was forced to slash its 2026 growth forecast to a meager 1–1.75% while watching inflation spike to 3.9% in May, driven almost entirely by energy costs. The central bank admits the oil shock has fundamentally weakened household consumption and investment. 

France saw its economy stall completely in the first quarter — zero growth — as exports collapsed 3.8%. The conflict is expected to shave 0.3 percentage points off annual growth, leaving the eurozone's second-largest economy limping along at just 0.7% for the year. 

The global bill is staggering: Moody's estimates the war has cost U.S. consumers and taxpayers $132 billion so far, while Pentagon operational spending alone hit $29 billion . The global economy just discovered its “stability guarantee” was made of paper—and signed in disappearing ink.

“The world order has shifted, and the economy is unlikely to simply return to where it was before the United States and Israel began bombing Iran… The war has set off a chain of changes that will be difficult to reverse,” The New York Times reports.

Funny how “stability” always works—right until the missiles ship.

Washington sold itself for decades as the adult in the room, the security provider, the invisible hand guiding tankers through the Gulf like a logistics deity. Then came the airstrikes, and suddenly the deity looked more like a volatility index with a flag.

Europe and Asia got the memo fast. Not the official one—the market one. Energy “diversification” is now code for: never again trust a chokepoint guarded by someone who might bomb it tomorrow. Renewable energy isn’t just green anymore; it’s geopolitical insurance.

Meanwhile, oil didn’t disappear. It just became political theater with a price tag. Every barrel now carries a surcharge: risk, fear, and a whisper that the next disruption is already scheduled.

The ceasefire framework? Sure, a nice press release. A temporary patch on a system that just proved it can’t reboot to its old settings.

So here’s the new global economy: less trust, more hedging, and a quiet realization that the “rules-based order” behaves more like a startup pivoting mid-crisis.

If the guarantor of stability is also the main source of shock, who exactly is the insurance for?
